note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Active runner training for a marathon with 2-week history of right knee pain and clicking provoked by running and repetitive knee flexion/extension; no instability or locking. Working impression: overuse knee injury—most consistent with iliotibial band friction syndrome vs patellofemoral pain; meniscal pathology less likely. Single transient episode of right toe tingling post-run.

History:
- Presenting complaint/timeline: Right knee pain and clicking for ~2 weeks, worsens during runs after ~20 minutes (~2.5–3 miles). Pain led to stopping the last run. Clicking noted during gym ab exercises requiring repeated knee flexion/extension. No pain at rest currently.
- Associated symptoms/review of systems:
  - Initial mild swelling after first run resolved with ice; currently no swelling.
  - No giving way, no locking, full ability to flex/extend, no difficulty with stairs or walking.
  - Single episode of tingling in right toes after a run; no persistent numbness/weakness. Occasional sock indentation after prolonged standing. No calf pain, redness, warmth, color/temperature change in legs.
  - No other joint pains; no back pain; no foot arch pain.
- Pertinent negatives: No fever/systemic symptoms; no persistent swelling, warmth, or redness; no gait limitation; no morning stiffness reported.
- Past medical history: Farsighted; prior LASIK surgery. Remote severe UTI (evaluated in ER). Otherwise healthy.
- Medications: PRN ibuprofen (up to 400 mg), sometimes uses naproxen (Aleve); vitamin D; melatonin; occasional alprazolam (Xanax). Occasional cannabis use.
- Allergies: Not stated.
- Social/preventive: Training for a marathon (recent increase in running volume; doing 4–8 mile runs). Plays sports including ice hockey (fall months ago with bruise, no ongoing knee issues). Lives in London.

Examination:
- Telemedicine visit; no vitals recorded.
- Patient-reported findings: Right knee currently not swollen; full range of motion; no locking or instability; pain localizes centrally with possible lateral emphasis (right side of right knee). Clicking occurs with repetitive flexion/extension during gym exercises. Ambulates and uses stairs without pain when not running.

Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Overuse-related right knee pain.
  - Iliotibial band friction syndrome (most likely): Lateral-predominant pain beginning after several miles of running, recent training increase, and clicking with repetitive flexion/extension; no locking/instability; symptoms improve with rest/ice.
  - Patellofemoral pain syndrome (possible): Pain with running and flexion/extension activities and clicking/crepitus; localization not clearly anterior and no stair pain reported.
  - Meniscal pathology (less likely): Clicking and one episode of post-activity swelling could fit; argued against by lack of locking, giving way, joint line tenderness, or clear twisting injury.
- Transient right toe tingling post-run: Likely benign/transient (e.g., footwear/lacing or minor nerve irritation); not primary driver of knee symptoms.

Plan:
- Symptomatic management:
  - Continue ice therapy regularly.
  - Reduce running volume/intensity; avoid running through pain. Pause runs if pain forces stopping.
  - Prescription for a stronger anti-inflammatory sent to pharmacy; take with food; do not combine with ibuprofen. (Specific medication not specified in consult.)
- Referrals/next steps:
  - Refer to physiotherapy for comprehensive knee assessment and initial management.
  - Consider in-clinic evaluation if physiotherapy wait is long or symptoms persist/worsen; imaging may be considered to evaluate intra-articular structures (e.g., cartilage/meniscus) based on exam findings.
- Safety-net/return precautions:
  - Seek urgent care if persistent swelling, heat, redness, fever/feeling unwell, or if the knee locks and cannot bend/straighten.
- Follow-up:
  - Not specified in consult; patient advised to arrange physiotherapy and to contact clinic if access is delayed or symptoms escalate.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements:
  - Drug allergies not documented.
  - Specific name/dose and instructions for the prescribed anti-inflammatory not documented.
  - Exact current OTC dosing/frequency (ibuprofen/naproxen) unclear.
  - No vitals or physical exam maneuvers performed due to telemedicine.
  - Formal follow-up interval not specified.
  - Social history (tobacco/alcohol), occupation, and baseline activity/footwear details not recorded.
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None significant. DDx emphasizes IT band vs patellofemoral pain; consistent with transcript. Diagnosis not confirmed due to lack of exam.
● Transcript quality:
  - Adequate for history; limited by absence of physical examination and vitals. Some medication details uncertain (patient unsure about Aleve’s active ingredient).
